Pre-launch starter guide to Japanese Ramen Simulator: the first-day shop flow from mise en place to counter service, plus solo play with part-time staff. Built from the official Wild Dog trailer and press coverage.
The first-day loop Read the shop layout → prep toppings and stock → boil and strain fresh noodles → paint your menu board → open the doors and work the counter → close out the day.
Opening the doors before mise en place is done. Once customers sit down there is no pause button — have chashu, toppings, and noodles portioned first.
Stacking every crew member on one station. Up to six players share one shop, so split cooking, noodles, and counter service into separate roles.
Ignoring shop safety. The developer confirms thieves and kitchen fires — keep a fire extinguisher within reach during service.

The game is not out yet — the planned Early Access start of Sept 28, 2026 at 9:00 AM JST was delayed, with no new date announced. The official 46-second announcement trailer is no longer the only footage: the Steam store description embeds seven in-engine gameplay clips of 2.5–6.3 seconds each. Everything on this page comes from that trailer, the store-page description and press coverage, and will be updated once Early Access launches.

Before your first customer sits down, walk the whole floor. Counter seats line an L-shaped counter facing an open kitchen, with a back kitchen for broth and prep. Up to six players share this space, so agree on who owns the cooking line, the noodle pot, and the counter before doors open.

Do your prep while the shop is still quiet: slice and portion chashu, green onion, and toppings, and keep your soup base hot. When the first wave walks in, a bowl should need only assembly — not cooking from scratch.

The trailer shows the noodle work done by hand: portion fresh noodles into a wire basket, boil, and shake them dry. Noodles set the pace of every bowl — in co-op, keep one owner on the noodle station so timing stays consistent.

The game ships with a full drawing board: brushes, color sliders, and vertical text tools for designing your own shop sign and menu board. Use it — a clear board tells customers what you sell before they even sit down.

Customers take counter stools and order; you boil, assemble, and slide bowls down the counter. The loop is: take the order, build the bowl, serve it hot, and free the seat for the next guest. In co-op, hand bowls to a teammate instead of running them yourself.

Your exterior works too: the wall plaque hangs on "preparing" until you are ready, then flips to greet guests, while the lanterns and street front give the shop its identity. Check the entrance before every shift so passers-by never mistake your shop for closed.

You do not need five friends to run this shop: the developer confirms solo owners can hire part-time staff to cover empty stations. In the trailer a full crew streams through the front door with name tags over their heads — online, those are friends; solo, hired help fills the same slots.

The official in-engine store clip catches the exact moment a shop day starts: a staff member hangs the wooden "open" sign by the entrance while name-tagged customers dash inside (image below). That sign is the start of the core loop — flip the sign, greet the rush, take orders, boil and build bowls, serve, clear, reset the seat, and keep it spinning until close. Two things come before anything else on day one: hang the sign, and get the pots hot.

What unlocks at each level in Japanese Ramen Simulator? Beer at 5, critics at 7, then miso, gyoza, chashu — the full unlock ladder from creator preview runs.

Japanese Ramen Simulator does not hand you the whole restaurant on day one — it hands you one rung of the kitchen at a time, and both creator preview runs behind this guide climbed it the same way: end the day in bed, get graded out of 1,000 the next morning, and wake up to a new ingredients & tools panel. The shops themselves are level-gated from the first minute, beer rolls in around level 5, and level 7 sends a critic you must impress before miso opens. One caveat up front: the game was scheduled for Steam Early Access on September 28, 2026, but that launch was delayed with no new date announced — everything below comes from creator preview builds.
End the day at the dorm bed; the morning RESULT screen grades service speed and taste out of 500 points each, then lists the ingredients and tools you just unlocked
The Kitchen Store stocks the beer server and keg flagged NEW at $0.00 around level 5; level 7 is a critics-only day, and passing it is what unlocks miso sauce
Kanzalone’s solo Normal run finished day 10 at level 12 (partitions, two-burner stove, desk, fan); Home Store decor stays locked up to levels 14-15, so more levels sit above

Every image on this page is a single frame from creator gameplay: the Japanese run by channel ホワイト, plus two late-game frames from Kanzalone’s English run (facecam cropped out), each linked with a timestamp to the exact moment in the source video. The level-to-unlock mapping is what these two preview builds showed — it is creator-observed, not an official table, and both runs were played on pre-Early-Access code, so details may change at or after launch. The game was scheduled to enter Steam Early Access on September 28, 2026; that date was delayed via a Steam announcement and a new date has not been announced. This page will be re-verified against the live build at launch.

Both preview runs open the same way. Difficulty defaults to Easy — Normal layers time pressure on top of it. Kanzalone switched to Normal before day one, while ホワイト started on Easy and flipped to Normal midweek once the loop felt comfortable. Next is the camera pick: first-person FPS or over-the-shoulder TPS, and the prompt itself says you can change it any time from the options menu. The part worth remembering is what these settings do not touch: the unlock ladder. Progression runs on the same rail either way — difficulty only changes how hard each shift pushes back, never what you unlock. Do not burn setup time on it.

Before the first bowl is ordered, the game shows its teeth. The Food Market hands you $500, a thin noodle box, pork bones, shoyu tare and a free green onion — and then a grid of padlocked cards: garlic and cabbage at level 1, menma at level 2, small green onion and bean sprouts at level 4, miso sauce at level 8, gyoza at level 10. The Home Store is stricter still: lightbulbs wait for level 14, wall scrolls and lanterns for level 15. So the day-one shop is not a menu — it is a table of contents for the next couple of weeks. Buy what is open, note what is coming, and stop reading the level locks as paywalls. They are this page’s progression chart, shown in-game.

There is no level-up button. You work the day, walk to the dorm bed and confirm 終了する (end day). The morning RESULT screen grades two bars — service speed and taste, 500 points each — stamps a rank, then drops the reward panel: 新食材&道具をゲット (new ingredients & tools). The frame here is the level 3 morning: chopsticks, table condiments, a table menu, tissues, an order holder and a noodle boiler for your staff, all in one drop. Not every night pays out — ホワイト logged at least one night where the level did not move, and while the HUD level badge carries an experience bar, the game never explains its rules. Treat sleep as the trigger and the scores as the throttle: the ladder advances on most overnights, not all.

The early levels are small, but they change how the shop feels. Level 2 unlocks menma in the Food Market — the entire haul of ホワイト’s level 2 — and, more importantly, right-clicking the register now offers バイト (part-time work). The hiring screen lines candidates up on clipboards at $5.00 per hour with an assign-location field, while a fourth slot stays padlocked until level 3. Reach level 3 and the padlock opens while the morning panel adds chopsticks and table condiments — until then, customers genuinely have no chopsticks, a gap ホワイト milked for jokes all stream. One hire on the register is the single biggest quality-of-life unlock of the first week; our staff hiring guide covers the assignment options.

Level 5 is the first level that feels like a second business. The Kitchen Store refreshes with a NEW wave: a cutting board, a kitchen knife — and in the same shipment, kunai and shuriken for the register thief — plus the beer server and the beer keg, both flagged $0.00 with a 初回無料 (first one free) tag. From the next morning the shop posts beer-order banners, beer glasses join the restock list, and pouring becomes a skill of its own: fill the mug, then right-click to top up the foam, or the order comes back. Both preview runs treat this as the money pivot — drink orders stack onto every ramen, and Kanzalone’s average ticket climbs from the low $20s past $35. Our beer pouring guide drills the foam timing.

Level 7 does not unlock an item; it unlocks an exam. The morning brief introduces the ラーメン評論家 (ramen critic) with a single instruction: serve ramen with elevated umami, aroma and color. For the whole day, only critics sit down — Kanzalone’s banner reads “only critics will visit today,” and he worked the entire day for a single guest. The verdict cuts both ways: his first tonkotsu shoyu was judged to “fall short,” its umami rating “just seven out of eight,” while ホワイト’s bowl earned “the soup’s flavor and aroma are perfect, the colors are vibrant, the overall balance is good.” Passing opens step 7; failing means another week on the same menu. On this day, build the broth for the brief, not for the regulars.

The morning after a passed critic visit, the reward panel looks different: 新食材&道具をゲット lists 味噌ダレ (miso sauce) under ingredients, the 本日のラーメン board now carries two recipes — tonkotsu shoyu and tonkotsu miso — and grated garlic joins the topping tray. Practically, this is the two-broth upgrade: Kanzalone immediately budgets a second pot so shoyu and miso broths run side by side, and prices climb with it — his miso bowls sell at $35 against $22 for shoyu. ホワイト also banked a critic’s trophy for the shelf. If step 6 was the exam, this is the diploma: a second flavor line that doubles the menu without doubling the kitchen.

The middle of the ladder turns the shop sideways. Around level 9, the morning panel adds gyoza as an ingredient along with a gyoza plate, a gyoza grill and order monitor stands. Kanzalone notes the grill never touches the menu board — gyoza ride along as a side to ramen orders: frozen onto the griddle, browned, held warm, served on the tray. One level later the game starts asking instead of offering: at level 10 the checklist reads “check shop expansion,” pointing you to the terminal and the shop expansion page — more windows, more seating, more kitchen. Kanzalone’s verdict after eyeing twenty tables: “there is absolutely no way, not by myself.” Expansion changes your floor plan; the gyoza line itself is walked through in our side dishes guide.

The last stretch of the observed ladder moves the shop upmarket. Level 11 delivers raw pork loin and a simmering pot, then walks you through chashu with a checklist: four pieces of pork loin into the pot, add water, add shoyu tare, place it on the stove and let it simmer — then slice it into the bowl. Kanzalone’s ticket climbs to $44 and he calls it “getting close to the $50.” Level 12, reached on day 10 of his Normal solo run, rounds the shop out with partition panels, a two-burner stove, an office desk and a fan. Past that, the preview runs stop proving things — but the Home Store’s level 14-15 locks say the ladder keeps going. When Early Access finally opens, this page gets re-verified against the live build.

No official number exists. The deepest proven point is level 12 — Kanzalone’s preview run reached it on day 10, solo on Normal — and the Home Store catalog lists decorations locked behind level 14 and level 15, so the ladder clearly continues above 12. Treat anything past 12 as unexplored until the full release.

Around level 5 in both preview runs. The Kitchen Store posts the beer server and beer keg flagged NEW at $0.00 (the first of each is free), beer glasses join the restock list, and customers start ordering beer with their ramen. Pouring it well is its own skill: fill the mug, then top up the foam.

Level 7, by both creators’ clocks. Critic day is a gate, not a gift: only critics visit, the brief demands high umami, aroma and color, and passing is what unlocks miso sauce and the second broth. A first attempt can fail — Kanzalone’s critic scored his bowl seven out of eight on umami and called it short.

The only observed trigger is ending the day: walk to the dorm bed and confirm. Levels land on most overnights but not all of them, and the morning score — service speed plus taste, 500 points each — is the closest thing to a visible throttle: keep both bars full by serving fast bowls that match the order. Hiring part-timers keeps the line moving, which is how both runs kept their scores maxed. No confirmed grind or XP farm exists beyond that.
